entities.name: Vandal Kingdom
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Vandal Kingdom (429–534 CE), established when King Genseric led approximately 80,000 Vandals across the Strait of Gibraltar into North Africa, controlled the former Roman province of Africa Proconsularis (modern Tunisia) for 105 years — cutting off Rome's grain supply, sacking Rome itself in 455 CE (giving 'vandalism' to the English language), and controlling the western Mediterranean sea lanes. The Vandal kingdom was destroyed in 533-534 CE by Belisarius's Byzantine reconquest in what remains the fastest conquest of a major kingdom in military history.

Genseric's crossing of North Africa (429-439 CE) — marching 3,000 km from Morocco to Carthage — was one of the most audacious movements of the Migration Period. The capture of Carthage (439 CE) gave Genseric control of Rome's primary grain supply and the most important western Mediterranean port. The Vandal fleet became the dominant naval power in the western Mediterranean — sacking Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, and the Balearic Islands.

The 455 CE sack of Rome — invited by Empress Eudoxia who opposed Petronius Maximus's seizure of power — lasted 14 days and removed enormous treasures including the Jewish menorah from the Temple of Jerusalem (taken by Titus in 70 CE, then taken by Vandals). The 533-534 CE Byzantine reconquest under Belisarius — defeating the Vandal army at the Battle of Ad Decimum and capturing King Gelimer in just one year — was so swift that contemporaries called it miraculous. The Vandals disappeared from history within a generation of conquest.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Vandal Kingdom's 455 CE Rome sack — which gave English the word 'vandalism' and removed the Jewish Temple menorah — and Belisarius's impossibly swift reconquest make it the kingdom that most shaped Roman decline mythology and Byzantine military reputation.
